factors.factor: Architecture with a single primary and a hot-standby secondary used only for failover: all load fell on one database, and the primary was a single point of failure with no usable alternative path during the incident.
factors.evidence: "In this setup a single database has to handle all the load, which is not ideal." and "db1.cluster.gitlab.com being a single point of failure." | "Due to the increased load, our PostgreSQL secondary's replication process started to lag behind."

factors.factor: Replication was not backed by WAL archiving, so once the secondary fell behind, it could only be re-synchronised manually
factors.evidence: "As GitLab.com was not using WAL archiving, the secondary had to be re-synchronised manually."

factors.factor: A background job for a hard-delete account removal was accidentally scheduled after an abuse flag, adding unplanned load during the spam-driven load spike.
factors.evidence: "part of the load was caused by a background job trying to remove a GitLab employee and their associated data... accidentally scheduled for removal."

factors.factor: Runbooks and upstream documentation did not describe that pg_basebackup silently waits before replication starts, so a normal waiting state was mistaken for a fault and re-sync troubleshooting was prolonged.
factors.evidence: "this is normal behaviour: pg_basebackup will wait for the primary to start sending over replication data... this was not clearly documented in our engineering runbooks nor in the official pg_basebackup document."

factors.factor: max_connections had been set far too high (8000) and was never reviewed, which blocked a PostgreSQL restart when max_wal_senders was raised and delayed the re-sync.
factors.evidence: "Such a value is way too high, yet it had been applied almost a year ago and was working fine until that point."

factors.factor: No safeguards or host-role confirmation existed for destructive operations such as wiping a data directory, so it was possible to run the operation on the primary while believing it was the secondary.
factors.evidence: "an engineer proceeds to wipe the PostgreSQL database directory, errantly thinking they were doing so on the secondary. Unfortunately this process was executed on the primary instead."

factors.factor: The backup job ran pg_dump 9.2 against PostgreSQL 9.6 (Omnibus defaulted to 9.2 on a non-database host), so every backup failed and no usable backups existed; this was not detected because failure notifications never arrived (see also the cronjob email/DMARC gap).
factors.evidence: "the backup procedure was using pg_dump 9.2, while our database is running PostgreSQL 9.6" and "we were never aware of the backups failing, until it was too late." | "DMARC was not enabled for the cronjob emails, resulting in them being rejected by the receiver."

factors.factor: Disaster recovery relied on snapshots and backups not designed for recovery; Azure disk snapshots were not enabled for database servers and LVM snapshots were not meant for DR
factors.evidence: "While enabled for the NFS servers, these snapshots were not enabled for any of the database servers as we assumed that our other backup procedures were sufficient enough." and "the produced snapshots are not really meant to be used for disaster recovery."

factors.factor: Staging environment used slow, cheap storage, making restoration bottlenecked by disk throughput
factors.evidence: "For our staging environment we were using Azure classic, without Premium Storage... the disks are very slow, resulting in them being the main bottleneck in the restoration process."

factors.factor: Recovery procedures were not tested or rehearsed, and there was no defined recovery path or coordination process, so locating and using backups failed and the team relied on ad hoc requests for help.
factors.evidence: "Hoping they could restore the database the engineers involved went to look for the database backups, and asked for help on Slack. Unfortunately the process of both finding and using backups failed completely."

action_items.action: Enable WAL archiving for the production PostgreSQL cluster so replicas can catch up from archived segments instead of requiring manual re-synchronisation.
Enable automated Azure disk snapshots and regular verified pg_dump/base backups for all database servers, with restore tests run on a schedule.
Fix the backup procedure to use the pg_dump binary matching the production PostgreSQL major version, and fail loudly when versions mismatch.
Add monitoring and alerting that verifies a successful backup has completed within the expected window and pages on absence, rather than relying on cronjob emails.
Enable DMARC for the email domain used by cronjob and system notifications so failure alerts are delivered.
Add safeguards to destructive database operations, such as hostname/role checks and an explicit confirmation step that verifies the target is the secondary before wiping a data directory.
Review and correct the max_connections setting and document a standard configuration review process for PostgreSQL parameters.
Document pg_basebackup's silent waiting behaviour in the engineering runbooks and create a tested, step-by-step replica rebuild runbook.

Write a disaster-recovery runbook for the production database and run restore drills at least quarterly, recording the results; include a defined incident coordination channel and roles so recovery does not depend on ad hoc requests for help.
Scale out database load by evaluating read replicas or query load balancing, reducing the single primary as a single point of failure.
Fix the account-removal background job so flagged accounts are not scheduled for hard deletion, and add rate limits to bulk deletion jobs.
Upgrade staging database storage to premium disks or otherwise ensure restore throughput is sufficient to meet recovery time objectives.
